T1001.description: Obfuscate C2 traffic by adding junk data, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols to evade detection and content analysis.

T1001.001.description: Append, prepend, or insert random/meaningless characters into C2 protocol traffic to defeat signature-based decoding and pattern analysis.

T1001.002.description: Hide C2 data or commands within digital media files (images, documents) transferred between systems to conceal communications.

T1001.003.description: Disguise C2 traffic by mimicking legitimate protocols/services (SSL/TLS, HTTP, Gmail, Google Drive) via spoofed headers, certificates, and URIs.

T1003.description: Extract account credentials (hashes or plaintext) from OS caches, memory, or databases to enable lateral movement and privileged access.

T1003.001.description: Dump LSASS process memory via procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or Mimikatz sekurlsa to extract logon credentials, hashes, and Kerberos tickets.

T1003.002.description: Extract local account hashes from SAM database via registry hive saves (reg save HKLM\sam) or in-memory tools requiring SYSTEM access.

T1003.003.description: Copy Active Directory database (NTDS.dit) from domain controllers using ntdsutil, VSS, or Invoke-NinjaCopy to extract all domain hashes.

T1003.004.description: Extract LSA secrets from HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets registry or memory using Mimikatz/Reg to recover service account credentials.

T1003.005.description: Extract cached domain logon hashes (DCC2/MS-Cache v2) from Windows registry or Linux SSSD/Quest caches; requires cracking, no pass-the-hash.

T1003.006.description: Abuse Domain Controller replication API (GetNCChanges/DRSUAPI) to simulate DC and pull password hashes from Active Directory, including KRBTGT, enabling Golden Ticket forging.

T1003.007.description: Search Linux /proc/<PID>/maps and /mem pseudo-filesystem entries for credential patterns or cleartext passwords cached in process memory.

T1003.008.description: Read and dump Linux /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow files to extract password hashes for offline cracking with tools like unshadow and John.

T1005.description: Search local file systems, configs, databases, VM files, and process memory for sensitive data prior to exfiltration using shell or CLI tools.

T1006.description: Read or write files directly from a logical volume by parsing raw file system structures, bypassing Windows file access controls and file monitoring, e.g. NinjaCopy or shadow-copy utilities.

T1007.description: Enumerate registered services and scheduled tasks using native OS commands to inform follow-on behaviors and target assessment.

T1008.description: Use alternate or backup communication channels when primary C2 is unavailable to maintain reliable control and avoid transfer thresholds.

T1010.description: Enumerate open application window titles via Native API or shell commands to identify user activity, target data, and security tools.

T1011.description: Exfiltrate data over a network medium separate from the C2 channel (WiFi, cellular, modem, RF) to bypass enterprise network monitoring.

T1011.001.description: Exfiltrate data via Bluetooth communication channel instead of primary C2, leveraging physical proximity and unmonitored RF transport.

T1012.description: Query Windows Registry via reg utility or APIs to enumerate OS configuration, installed software, and security settings to shape follow-on actions.

T1014.description: Hide presence of files, processes, services, and network connections by intercepting and modifying OS API calls at user, kernel, hypervisor, or firmware level.

T1016.description: Enumerate IP/MAC addresses, routes, and interfaces using OS utilities or network device CLI to map network configuration.

T1016.001.description: Test Internet connectivity via ping, tracert, or HTTP GET to confirm system can reach C2 infrastructure before connecting.

T1016.002.description: Enumerate saved Wi-Fi SSIDs and passwords via netsh wlan, wlanAPI.dll, /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections, or macOS security command.

T1018.description: Enumerate remote hosts by IP/hostname via net view, ping, host files, ARP cache, or network device CLI to identify lateral movement targets.

T1020.description: Automate data transfer out of network via scripts or scheduled processes, typically combined with C2 channel or alternative protocol exfiltration.

T1020.001.description: Abuse native traffic mirroring features on network devices or cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure) to duplicate and redirect network traffic to attacker infrastructure.

T1021.description: Authenticate to remote services accepting interactive logins using valid credentials to execute actions as logged-on user across hosts.

T1021.001.description: Log into systems via RDP/RDS using valid credentials for interactive GUI access, often combined with accessibility feature backdoors for persistence.

T1021.002.description: Authenticate to remote Windows systems via SMB to access hidden admin shares (C$/ADMIN$/IPC$) for file transfer and remote execution using valid accounts or NTLM hashes.

T1021.003.description: Invoke remote COM objects via DCOM/RPC to execute code on remote hosts, abusing methods in Office apps, MMC20.Application, or ShellWindows for lateral movement.

T1021.004.description: Authenticate to remote hosts via SSH using passwords or keypairs to obtain interactive shell access; on ESXi enabled via vim-cmd or vCenter.

T1021.005.description: Connect to remote systems via VNC/RFB protocol for graphical desktop control, relaying screen/keyboard/mouse input to execute actions as logged-on user.

T1021.006.description: Use WinRM service/protocol to remotely execute commands, modify registry/services on Windows hosts; commonly invoked via PowerShell remoting or winrm command.

T1021.007.description: Authenticate to cloud services using federated/synchronized on-prem identities via web console or CLI to access cloud control plane and resources.

T1021.008.description: Access cloud-hosted VMs directly via native provider interfaces (Azure Serial Console, EC2 Instance Connect, AWS SSM) often granting SYSTEM/root level console access.

T1025.description: Enumerate and collect files from removable media (USB, optical drives) connected to compromised hosts, often via cmd or automated collection scripts prior to exfiltration.

T1027.description: Encrypt, encode, compress, or obfuscate file contents, scripts, or commands to evade signature-based detection, static analysis, and application controls.

T1027.001.description: Append junk bytes to binaries to alter file hash and inflate size beyond AV/sandbox scan limits, evading hash blocklists and static signatures without changing functionality.

T1027.002.description: Compress or encrypt executables to alter file signatures and evade signature-based detection; decompression occurs in memory at runtime.

T1027.003.description: Hide data or code within digital media files (images, audio, video) to conceal payloads or exfiltrated information from detection.

T1027.004.description: Deliver payloads as uncompiled source code that is compiled on the victim host via native compilers, bypassing executable-focused defenses.

T1027.005.description: Modify detected tools by removing or altering indicators (hashes, signatures, strings) so updated versions evade defensive detections.

T1027.006.description: Embed payloads inside HTML files using JavaScript Blobs or Data URLs that reconstruct malicious files client-side, bypassing web content filters.

T1027.007.description: Resolve Windows API function addresses at runtime via hashes/identifiers instead of static imports to hide functionality from IAT analysis.

T1027.008.description: Remove symbols, strings, and debug info from binaries or scripts to hinder reverse engineering and static analysis.

T1027.009.description: Conceal malicious payloads inside otherwise benign files (overlays, nested executables, scripts) to hide content and preserve trust signatures.

T1027.010.description: Obfuscate command-line strings via encoding, escape chars, concatenation, casing tricks, or path traversal to evade signature detection.

T1027.011.description: Store payloads or data in non-file locations like Registry, WMI, event logs, or shared memory tmpfs to evade file-based scanning.

T1027.012.description: Abuse LNK file icon location metadata field to download remote payloads via external URLs, bypassing content filters when shortcut is invoked.

T1027.013.description: Encrypt or encode file contents using hardcoded keys, Base64, password-protected archives, or SFX stubs to evade static signature detection until runtime decoding.

T1027.014.description: Mutate code footprint at each execution while preserving functionality, defeating signature-based antivirus through self-modifying binaries and mutation engines.

T1027.015.description: Compress payloads using ZIP/gzip/7z/RAR formats, including concatenated archives that confuse parsers, to obfuscate content and bypass detection in transit.

T1027.016.description: Insert non-functional instructions like NOP (0x90) or dead code branches into malware to impede static analysis and signature-based detection.

T1027.017.description: Embed malicious JavaScript inside SVG image files via XML script tags to assemble/download payloads, redirect users, or display fake forms past content filters.

T1027.018.description: Hide payloads using non-rendering Unicode characters (zero-width, PUA, bidi controls) decoded at runtime via eval or Proxy traps to evade visual and static inspection.

T1029.description: Schedule data exfiltration at specific times or intervals to blend with normal traffic patterns and business activity rhythms.

T1030.description: Split exfiltrated data into fixed-size chunks or limit packet sizes below DLP/network monitoring thresholds to avoid volume-based alerts.

T1033.description: Identify primary, current, or active users via whoami, who, w, dscl, environment variables, or network device show users commands to shape follow-on actions.

T1036.description: Manipulate artifact features (name, location, metadata, signatures) to appear legitimate or benign, evading user scrutiny and security tools.

T1036.001.description: Copy signing metadata from legitimate signed binaries onto unsigned payloads. Signature fails validation but appears legitimate to users and improperly configured tools.

T1036.002.description: Insert RTLO Unicode character (U+202E) in filenames to reverse displayed text, disguising executables (e.g., scr) as benign types (e.g., docx).

T1036.003.description: Rename or relocate legitimate system binaries (rundll32, PsExec) before execution to bypass detections keyed on utility names or standard paths.

T1036.004.description: Assign scheduled tasks or services names/descriptions resembling legitimate ones to blend with benign system activity.

T1036.005.description: Name or place files, registry keys, or container resources to mimic trusted system locations or legitimate program names.

T1036.006.description: Append space to filename so OS identifies true file type via magic bytes rather than extension, causing executable handling of seemingly benign files.

T1036.007.description: Use double extensions (e.g., Evil.txt.exe) where OS hides the true second extension, tricking users into executing payloads disguised as documents/images.

T1036.008.description: Modify file header bytes, extension, or icon to disguise payload as benign type (e.g., PHP backdoor as .gif), bypassing validation and sanitization.

T1036.009.description: Sever parent-child process relationship via double fork() or daemon() syscall so payload is reparented to PID 1, evading process-tree-based detections.

T1036.010.description: Create or rename accounts to match legitimate or generic names (admin, root, backup, service accounts) to blend new accounts among existing ones.

T1036.011.description: Overwrite argv memory region of running Linux process with null bytes and spoofed command string to hide original invocation in /proc/PID/cmdline and ps output.

T1036.012.description: Spoof browser/system attributes such as User-Agent, OS, language, timezone, and resolution to mimic legitimate client traffic and evade fingerprint-based detection.

T1037.description: Register scripts that run automatically at system boot or user logon to establish persistence and potentially execute with elevated privileges.

T1037.001.description: Add script path to HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript registry key to execute upon Windows user logon for persistence.

T1037.002.description: Modify /Library/Preferences/com.apple.loginwindow.plist with LoginHook/LogoutHook key via defaults utility to run script as root on user logon/logout.

T1037.003.description: Assign logon scripts via Active Directory or Group Policy to execute on user logon across domain systems for persistence at user privileges.

T1037.004.description: Append malicious commands to Unix rc.local, rc.common, or ESXi local.sh executed as root at boot for persistence on Linux, ESXi, IoT systems.

T1037.005.description: Create a directory with an executable and StartupParameters.plist in /Library/StartupItems so the deprecated macOS startup item mechanism runs it as root at boot for persistence.

T1039.description: Search and collect sensitive files from mounted network shares, file servers, or shared directories accessible from compromised host prior to exfiltration.

T1040.description: Passively capture network traffic via promiscuous interfaces, span ports, or cloud traffic mirroring (AWS/GCP/Azure vTap) to harvest credentials, configurations, and protocol data.

T1041.description: Steal data by tunneling it through the existing command and control channel using the same protocol as C2 communications.

T1046.description: Enumerate services on remote hosts via port/vulnerability scanning or mDNS queries (Bonjour, dns-sd) to identify exploitable software and network topology.

T1047.description: Abuse WMI service via wmic.exe, COM APIs, or PowerShell to execute commands locally or remotely over DCOM (135) or WinRM (5985/5986).

T1048.description: Steal data via a protocol distinct from C2 (FTP, SMTP, HTTP/S, DNS, SMB) using utilities like curl, net, or cloud APIs.

T1048.001.description: Exfiltrate data over a non-C2 channel using symmetric encryption (RC4, AES) with shared keys, potentially layered over already-encrypted protocols.

T1048.002.description: Exfiltrate data over a non-C2 channel using asymmetric encryption protocols like HTTPS/TLS/SSL with public-private keypairs.

T1048.003.description: Exfiltrate data over unencrypted protocols (HTTP, FTP, DNS) optionally obfuscated via encoding like base64 or embedded in protocol headers.

T1049.description: Enumerate active network connections via netstat, net use/session, lsof, who, or ESXi/network device CLI commands to map connected systems.

T1052.description: Exfiltrate data via physical media such as USB drives or external storage, often to bridge air-gapped networks.

T1052.001.description: Copy data to USB-connected physical device for exfiltration, often bridging air-gapped networks or used as final exfil point between disconnected systems.

T1053.description: Abuse OS task scheduling utilities to execute code at specified times/startup for persistence, privilege escalation under specified accounts, or masking under trusted processes.

T1053.002.description: Abuse the at utility (Windows/Linux/macOS) to schedule code execution; on Linux can escape restricted shells or escalate via sudo; Windows requires Task Scheduler service.

T1053.003.description: Abuse Unix cron/crontab time-based scheduler to execute code at startup or recurring intervals for persistence; ESXi requires direct crontab file edits.

T1053.005.description: Abuse Windows Task Scheduler via schtasks, WMI PS_ScheduledTask, or netapi32 to execute code as SYSTEM; hide tasks by deleting Security Descriptor registry value.

T1053.006.description: Abuse systemd .timer unit files paired with .service units to schedule code execution at calendar/relative times for root or user-level persistence on Linux.

T1053.007.description: Abuse Kubernetes CronJob/Job resources to schedule container deployments executing malicious code across cluster nodes and maintain container quantities for persistence.

T1055.description: Inject arbitrary code into address space of live process to evade process-based defenses, access target memory/resources, and inherit privileges of host process.

T1055.001.description: Inject DLL into remote process via VirtualAllocEx/WriteProcessMemory/CreateRemoteThread calling LoadLibrary; variants include reflective DLL, memory module, and module stomping/hollowing.

T1055.002.description: Copy PE code into remote process virtual address space and invoke via new thread; requires remapping memory references since displacement differs from original.

T1055.003.description: Suspend existing process thread, unmap/hollow memory, write malicious code, realign thread context, then resume execution within legitimate process context.

T1055.004.description: Attach malicious code to thread's APC queue, executed when thread enters alertable state; variants include Early Bird (pre-entry-point) and AtomBombing (global atom table).

T1055.005.description: Manipulate TLS callback pointers in PE header to redirect execution to malicious code before the legitimate entry point is reached.

T1055.008.description: Attach to running process via ptrace syscall, write arbitrary code into memory and modify register/instruction pointer to execute; limited to child or lower-privilege processes.

T1055.009.description: Enumerate target process memory via /proc filesystem, craft ROP payload from discovered gadgets, then overwrite stack/memory mappings using dd to hijack execution.

T1055.011.description: Abuse 40-byte Extra Window Memory of registered window classes to store pointer to malicious code in shared sections; triggered via window procedure invocation, avoiding WriteProcessMemory/CreateRemoteThread.

T1055.012.description: Create new process in suspended state, unmap its image memory, write malicious code in its place, realign thread context, and resume execution masquerading as legitimate process.

T1055.013.description: Abuse Windows Transactional NTFS to overwrite legitimate file in transaction, load malicious section into memory, rollback file changes, then spawn process from tainted section.

T1055.014.description: Hijack syscall stubs in vdso shared object mapped into Linux processes, redirect via patched global offset table entries to load malicious shared object and execute syscalls.

T1055.015.description: Abuse list-view control callbacks via shatter-attack window messages; copy payload 2-bytes at a time via LVM_SETITEMPOSITION then trigger as ListView_SortItems callback.

T1056.description: Capture user input via keylogging, API hooking, GUI credential prompts, or web portal injection to harvest credentials and sensitive data.

T1056.001.description: Log user keystrokes via API hooks, raw hardware buffer reads, kernel drivers, registry modifications, or network device OS hooks to capture credentials.

T1056.002.description: Display spoofed OS or application credential dialogs (UAC, installer, browser auth) via AppleScript, PowerShell, or shell to trick users into entering credentials.

T1056.003.description: Inject code into externally-facing login portals (VPN, webmail) to log and exfiltrate credentials of authenticating users.

T1056.004.description: Hook Windows API or Linux/macOS library functions (via hook procedures, IAT, inline patching, LD_PRELOAD) to intercept credential parameters passed to authentication functions.

T1057.description: Enumerate running processes via tasklist, ps, Get-Process, /proc, esxcli system process list, or show processes to map software and inform follow-on actions.

T1059.description: Execute commands and scripts via built-in interpreters (cmd, PowerShell, bash, Python, JavaScript, VBScript) embedded in payloads or invoked interactively.

T1059.001.description: Execute PowerShell cmdlets and scripts for discovery, in-memory payload execution, and remoting; may bypass powershell.exe via System.Management.Automation DLL.

T1059.002.description: Execute AppleScript via osascript, NSAppleScript, or OSAScript to control macOS applications, send keystrokes, display fake dialogs, and invoke native APIs.

T1059.003.description: Execute commands and batch scripts via cmd.exe locally or over remote services for payload execution and interactive C2 shell operation.

T1059.004.description: Execute commands via Unix shells (sh/bash/zsh) interactively or through .sh scripts on Linux/macOS/ESXi; controls all system aspects, used for payload delivery and persistence.

T1059.005.description: Execute payloads via Visual Basic, VBA macros in Office documents, or VBScript on Windows; commonly embedded in spearphishing attachments to run malicious commands.

T1059.006.description: Execute commands via Python interpreter or .py scripts; leverage built-in packages for file I/O, downloads, and command execution; can be compiled to binaries.

T1059.007.description: Execute via JavaScript/JScript/JXA; run through Windows Script engine, browsers, HTA pages, or macOS osascript; used in drive-by compromises and obfuscated payloads.

T1059.008.description: Abuse network device command line interpreters to modify configs, manipulate traffic flows, load malicious firmware, or disable logging/security features.

T1059.009.description: Invoke cloud APIs via CLI, SDKs, or browser-based Cloud Shells to execute administrative actions across compute, IAM, storage, and security services.

T1059.010.description: Execute payloads via AutoIT (.au3) or AutoHotKey (.ahk) automation scripts on Windows; often compiled to standalone .exe and used for keyloggers or phishing payloads.

T1059.011.description: Execute Lua scripts via stand-alone interpreter or embedded lua_State in applications; adversaries replace or abuse existing Lua interpreters for runtime code execution.

T1059.012.description: Abuse ESXi hypervisor CLIs like esxcli and vim-cmd to manage VMs, modify firewall/log settings, and support discovery or ransomware encryption operations.

T1059.013.description: Use Docker CLI/SDK or Kubernetes kubectl/API to pull images, run containers, execute commands in containers, and enumerate pods, deployments, and namespaces.

T1068.description: Exploit software vulnerabilities in OS, kernel, or drivers to elevate privileges from user to SYSTEM/root or escape containers/VMs. Includes Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) for kernel-mode execution.

T1069.description: Enumerate group and permission settings to identify accounts, group membership, and elevated privileges for follow-on targeting.

T1069.001.description: Enumerate local system groups via commands like `net localgroup`, `dscl . -list /Groups`, or `groups` to identify privileged local accounts.

T1069.002.description: Enumerate domain-level groups using `net group /domain`, `ldapsearch`, or `dscacheutil -q group` to identify privileged domain accounts.

T1069.003.description: Enumerate cloud roles/groups via Get-MsolRole, `az ad user get-member-groups`, AWS ListRolePolicies, or Google Cloud Identity API to map cloud permissions and ACLs.

T1070.description: Selectively delete or modify forensic artifacts (logs, histories, metadata) to blend with legitimate activity and delay detection while preserving normal-looking system state.

T1070.003.description: Delete or modify shell command history (`history -c`, rm ~/.bash_history, Clear-History, ConsoleHost_history.txt) on Linux/macOS/Windows/network devices/ESXi to conceal executed commands.

T1070.004.description: Delete files dropped during intrusion using built-in commands (del, rm, unlink) or tools like SDelete to remove malware and tool traces.

T1070.005.description: Delete Windows network share or SMB admin share connections after use, typically via net use \\system\share /delete, to remove traces of lateral movement.

T1070.006.description: Modify file MACB timestamps via API ($SI) or kernel ($FN) on Windows, or `touch -a -m -t`/`touch -r` on Linux/ESXi, to blend malicious files with legitimate ones and evade forensic timeline analysis.

T1070.007.description: Delete network connection artifacts including RDP registry keys (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client), .rdp cache files, and Linux/macOS system logs to conceal remote session traces.

T1070.008.description: Delete emails, mailbox metadata, and export logs using tools like ExchangePowerShell, mail CLI, or AppleScript to erase evidence of phishing, collection, or email-based C2.

T1070.009.description: Remove persistence artifacts such as services, executables, registry run keys, plist files, or created accounts to eliminate traces of foothold mechanisms.

T1070.010.description: Copy/move malware payloads to new directories or rename them to blend with legitimate files, target AV exclusion paths, or separate artifacts from initial execution events.

T1071.description: Communicate over application layer protocols (web, mail, DNS, file transfer, pub/sub) to embed C2 commands within legitimate-looking traffic and evade network filtering.

T1071.001.description: Embed C2 traffic within HTTP/S or WebSocket requests/responses, hiding commands in headers, URIs, or body fields to blend with normal web browsing.

T1071.002.description: Tunnel C2 commands and data through file transfer protocols like SMB, FTP, FTPS, or TFTP, concealing payloads in protocol fields or transferred files.

T1071.003.description: Use email protocols (SMTP/S, POP3/S, IMAP) to carry C2 commands within message bodies, headers, or attachments, blending with normal mail traffic.

T1071.004.description: Tunnel C2 over DNS queries/responses, encoding commands in subdomains or TXT/A records; infrequent beaconing conceals traffic among normal DNS lookups.

T1071.005.description: Leverage pub/sub messaging protocols (MQTT, XMPP, AMQP, STOMP) with centralized brokers to relay C2 commands via topic subscriptions while mimicking IoT/messaging traffic.

T1072.description: Abuse centralized endpoint/configuration management platforms to push code execution across enterprise systems; enables mass lateral movement, on-prem command execution from cloud admin consoles, and broad payload deployment.

T1074.description: Collect and consolidate data into a central location or file prior to exfiltration to reduce C2 connections and aid evasion; may use cmd/bash copy operations.

T1074.001.description: Aggregate collected data into directories, databases, or Windows Registry on the local compromised system before exfiltration, often via cmd/bash copy commands.

T1074.002.description: Consolidate data from multiple compromised hosts onto a single internal system or cloud VM prior to exfiltration, reducing C2 connection volume and detection surface.

T1078.description: Obtain and use legitimate account credentials to access systems, bypass controls, and persist; minimizes malware footprint and pivots across local/domain/cloud account overlaps.

T1078.001.description: Authenticate using built-in or vendor-preset accounts (Guest, root, vpxuser, AWS root) with unchanged factory credentials to gain access to appliances, OS, or cloud platforms.

T1078.002.description: Compromise and use Active Directory domain user, admin, or service accounts—often via credential dumping or password reuse—to access privileged domain resources across systems.

T1078.003.description: Abuse local system accounts configured for user, service, or admin tasks; password reuse across hosts enables lateral movement and privilege escalation via dumped local creds.

T1078.004.description: Compromise cloud or federated/synced identity accounts to access SaaS/IaaS resources, pivot to on-prem via hybrid join, assume roles, or steal tokens from Managed Identities.

T1080.description: Plant malicious files, scripts, or trojanized binaries on network shares or code repos; includes directory .LNK pivot tricks and appending code to existing EXE/DLL/SCR/BAT/VBS files.

T1082.description: Enumerate OS version, patches, hotfixes, hardware, and architecture via built-in utilities, cloud APIs, or ESXi esxcli to shape follow-on payloads and actions.

T1083.description: Enumerate files and directories via shell utilities or Native API to locate target data and shape follow-on actions across hosts and network shares.

T1087.description: Enumerate valid accounts, usernames, or emails via built-in commands, cloud APIs, or file searches to support brute-force, phishing, or takeover.

T1087.001.description: Enumerate local system accounts via net, id, groups, /etc/passwd, dscl, or esxcli to identify users and groups on the host.

T1087.002.description: Enumerate domain accounts and groups via net /domain, ldapsearch, dscacheutil, or AD PowerShell cmdlets to identify privileged targets.

T1087.003.description: Enumerate email addresses by dumping Exchange Global Address Lists via PowerShell cmdlets or Google Workspace Directory queries.

T1087.004.description: Enumerate cloud user, role, and service accounts via AZ CLI, AWS IAM, GCP gcloud, or MSOnline PowerShell cmdlets.

T1090.description: Route C2 traffic through proxies or port redirectors to mask infrastructure, chain hops, and blend with trusted paths including CDNs.

T1090.001.description: Use compromised internal systems as proxies to relay C2 between infected hosts, often via p2p protocols like SMB, reducing external connections.

T1090.002.description: Use external intermediary hosts (VPS, cloud, compromised systems) as port redirectors to mask the true C2 destination from victim traffic.

T1090.003.description: Chain multiple proxies (Tor, ORB networks, P2P/blockchain, compromised routers with patched images) to obscure C2 traffic origin across multiple hops.

T1090.004.description: Exploit CDN routing by placing different domains in TLS SNI and HTTP Host headers so traffic appears destined for benign domain but routes to C2.

T1091.description: Copy malware to USB/removable media abusing Autorun or file renaming to spread to air-gapped systems or gain initial access via infected devices.

T1092.description: Relay C2 commands and files between Internet-connected and disconnected hosts via removable media shuttling between compromised systems.

T1095.description: Use non-application layer protocols (ICMP, UDP, SOCKS, VMCI on ESXi) for C2 to bypass monitoring focused on HTTP/TCP traffic.

T1098.description: Modify existing accounts (credentials, permissions, group membership) to preserve access, bypass password policies, or escalate privileges.

T1098.001.description: Add adversary-controlled credentials (SSH keys, access keys, service principal secrets, app passwords) to cloud accounts for persistence and MFA bypass.

T1098.002.description: Grant delegate or folder permissions (Add-MailboxPermission, Gmail delegation, Default/Anonymous folder rights) for persistent mailbox access.

T1098.003.description: Assign elevated cloud roles/IAM policies (global admin, AttachUserPolicy) to controlled accounts including external tenants for persistent privileged access.

T1098.004.description: Append adversary public keys to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (or via cloud add-metadata/PATCH APIs, network device CLI) for persistent SSH access.

T1098.005.description: Register adversary-controlled device to victim account via MFA self-enrollment or Entra ID join to bypass MFA/conditional access, enable intra-org spearphishing, and maintain persistence.

T1098.006.description: Bind additional Roles/ClusterRoles or modify ABAC policies in Kubernetes to grant controlled accounts elevated permissions for persistent cluster access.

T1098.007.description: Add accounts to privileged local/domain groups (Administrators, RDP Users, sudoers, VPN) via net/usermod commands to maintain elevated persistent access.

T1102.description: Relay C2 traffic through legitimate external web services to blend with expected network noise and protect back-end infrastructure via dynamic redirection.

T1102.001.description: Post obfuscated/encoded C2 domains or IPs on legitimate web services; infected hosts fetch and parse these to locate real C2 infrastructure.

T1102.002.description: Send commands and receive output through legitimate web services (forums, social media, Git) using posts/comments as bidirectional C2 channel.

T1102.003.description: Retrieve C2 commands from a legitimate web service or social media site without returning output over that channel, sending results elsewhere or not at all.

T1104.description: Use separate staged C2 servers where initial loader fetches second-stage RAT from distinct infrastructure, obfuscating full chain and enabling fallback.

T1105.description: Download tools/files from external systems into compromised host via utilities like certutil, PowerShell, curl, wget, scp, package managers, or cloud sync clients.

T1106.description: Invoke native OS API functions or direct syscalls (NtCreateProcess, CreateProcess, fork) to execute code while bypassing user-mode API hooks and EDR sensors.

T1110.description: Systematically guess passwords or crack obtained hashes against accounts via online services or offline against credential material to gain account access.

T1110.001.description: Iteratively guess passwords via common lists against management services (22,23,3389,445,389,88) or SSO/federated apps; risks account lockouts and logon failures.

T1110.002.description: Recover plaintext passwords offline from acquired hashes using dictionaries, rules, or rainbow tables; used when Pass-the-Hash unavailable.

T1110.003.description: Attempt one or few common passwords across many accounts to evade lockout thresholds; often throttled and targets LDAP/Kerberos to avoid 4625 events.

T1547.003.description: Register malicious DLL as subkey under HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\TimeProviders\ via DllName value, loaded by W32Time service as Local Service at boot.

T1547.004.description: Modify Winlogon Registry subkeys (Notify, Userinit, Shell) under HKLM/HKCU Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon to load malicious DLLs/executables at user logon for persistence.

T1547.005.description: Add malicious SSP DLLs via HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages registry keys to load into LSASS at boot, accessing plaintext credentials and persisting code execution.

T1547.006.description: Load malicious Loadable Kernel Modules (Linux) or kernel extensions (macOS kext) running at Ring 0 to hide processes/files, tamper logs, and establish rootkit persistence.

T1547.007.description: Add malicious application paths to ~/Library/Preferences/ByHost/com.apple.loginwindow.[UUID].plist so macOS automatically relaunches them when user logs back in after logout/restart.

T1547.008.description: Replace or add illegitimate LSASS drivers/DLLs loaded by lsass.exe to continuously execute payloads within the Local Security Authority subsystem process for persistence.

T1547.009.description: Create or modify .lnk shortcut files in startup folders or alter target paths to execute malicious payloads on boot/login, often combined with masquerading.

T1547.010.description: Register DLL via AddMonitor API or HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors Driver value; spoolsv.exe loads it at boot under SYSTEM privileges.

T1547.012.description: Install malicious print processor DLLs via AddPrintProcessor API or Print\Environments registry key; loaded by spoolsv.exe at boot under SYSTEM privileges.

T1547.013.description: Add or modify .desktop files in /etc/xdg/autostart or ~/.config/autostart with malicious Exec directive to launch payloads when XDG-compliant desktop environment loads at login.

T1547.014.description: Create registry key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components with malicious StubPath value executed in user context at logon for persistence.

T1547.015.description: Adds login items via shared file list or Service Management Framework to auto-execute payloads at user login through AppleScript or SMLoginItemSetEnabled API calls.

T1548.description: Circumvents built-in privilege elevation controls to gain higher-level permissions beyond what is authorized for the current user.

T1548.001.description: Abuses binaries with setuid/setgid bits set to execute code in the owner's privileged context, often via shell escapes from vulnerable SUID binaries.

T1548.002.description: Bypasses Windows UAC to elevate from medium to high integrity using auto-elevating binaries, COM objects, or DLL hijacking without prompting the user.

T1548.003.description: Abuses sudo caching or modifies sudoers file (e.g., NOPASSWD, disabling tty_tickets) to execute commands as root without re-entering passwords.

T1548.004.description: Calls deprecated AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API on macOS to prompt user for credentials and execute payloads as root without code integrity validation.

T1548.005.description: Abuses cloud JIT access, role impersonation, PassRole, or domain-wide delegation to temporarily gain elevated permissions distinct from the account's standard role.

T1548.006.description: Manipulates macOS TCC database or abuses already-permitted apps (e.g., Finder with FDA) to inherit privacy permissions for camera, microphone, or disk access.

T1550.description: Uses stolen hashes, Kerberos tickets, or access tokens to authenticate laterally without knowing plaintext passwords or supplying additional MFA factors.

T1550.001.description: Uses stolen OAuth or cloud API access tokens to authenticate to SaaS/cloud APIs, bypassing MFA and password resets via long-lived refresh tokens or federated sessions.

T1550.002.description: Authenticate as user using captured NTLM password hash without cleartext password, bypassing standard auth; can also generate Kerberos tickets via overpass-the-hash.

T1550.003.description: Authenticate to systems using stolen Kerberos service tickets or TGTs without password, enabling lateral movement to resources the ticket grants access to.

T1550.004.description: Import stolen authentication cookies into attacker-controlled browser to access web/cloud applications as victim, bypassing MFA since session is already authenticated.

T1552.description: Search compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials in files, registry, shell history, private keys, or application-specific repositories.

T1552.001.description: Search local and remote filesystems for files containing stored credentials including config files, source code, backups, and cloud/container credential files.

T1552.002.description: Query Windows Registry for stored credentials using commands like `reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s` to find passwords used by programs/autologons.

T1552.003.description: Read shell history files (bash, zsh, PowerShell PSReadline) for credentials passed as command-line parameters to programs.

T1552.004.description: Locate private key files (.key, .pem, .ppk, .pfx) in directories like ~/.ssh for authentication to remote services, decryption, or device impersonation.

T1552.005.description: Query cloud instance metadata API at 169.254.169.254 from compromised VM or via SSRF to extract IAM credentials and UserData secrets.

T1552.006.description: Search SYSVOL for GPP XML files containing cpassword field and decrypt with public AES key to recover local account passwords set via group policy.

T1552.007.description: Query container management APIs (Docker/Kubernetes) to harvest credentials, secrets, and logs containing authentication material from cluster components or cloud resources.

T1552.008.description: Extract credentials shared via communication platforms (chat, email, collaboration tools) by accessing endpoints, servers, admin portals, or automated workflow integrations.

T1553.description: Undermine OS/application trust mechanisms that warn or block untrusted code via permission changes, registry edits, or stolen signing certificates.

T1553.001.description: Strip or avoid the macOS com.apple.quarantine extended attribute to bypass Gatekeeper checks (code signing, notarization, policy) when launching downloaded apps.

T1553.002.description: Sign malware with acquired, stolen, or self-created code signing certificates to produce valid signatures that bypass execution policies requiring signed code.

T1553.003.description: Hijack Subject Interface Package or trust provider registry entries (CryptSIPDll* / FinalPolicy DLLs) to force WinVerifyTrust to return success for unsigned code.

T1553.004.description: Install adversary-controlled root certificate into trust store to suppress TLS warnings, enable AiTM interception, or validate malicious signed code.

T1553.005.description: Deliver payloads inside container formats (ISO, VHD, ARJ, GZIP) whose extracted contents don't inherit the NTFS Zone.Identifier ADS, evading SmartScreen and Protected View.

T1553.006.description: Disable signature enforcement (DSE/SIP) via bcdedit TESTSIGNING, csrutil disable, registry edits, or kernel memory patching of g_CiOptions through vulnerable signed drivers.

T1554.description: Modify legitimate host binaries (SSH/FTP/browser clients) with backdoors, IAT hooks, or patched entry points for persistence and credential capture; block updates via version locking.

T1555.description: Search common credential storage locations across OS and applications to extract stored usernames, passwords, and secrets for lateral movement.

T1555.001.description: Extract credentials from macOS Keychain files using security command or direct file reads, requiring user's login password to decrypt stored secrets.

T1555.002.description: Root-level scanning of securityd process memory on pre-El Capitan macOS to extract cached master key and decrypt keychain plaintext passwords.

T1555.003.description: Read browser credential databases (e.g. Chrome Login Data SQLite) and call CryptUnprotectData or scan process memory to recover saved website passwords.

T1555.004.description: Enumerate Windows Credential Manager Vaults via vaultcmd, CredEnumerateA API, or direct .vcrd file reads to extract stored application and website credentials.

T1555.005.description: Extract master password or decrypted entries from third-party password manager process memory or database files via memory scraping or brute force.

T1555.006.description: Request secrets from cloud-native vaults (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager) using compromised privileged cloud identities or service permissions.

T1556.description: Tamper with authentication components (LSASS, SAM, PAM, auth plugins) to harvest credentials or bypass validation enabling persistent unauthorized account access.

T1556.001.description: Patch LSASS on domain controllers (Skeleton Key) injecting a master password allowing authentication as any domain user until DC reboot.

T1556.002.description: Register malicious password filter DLL with LSA so it receives plaintext passwords during validation, harvesting credentials on each password change.

T1556.003.description: Modify PAM modules like pam_unix.so to accept hardcoded credentials as backdoor or harvest plaintext passwords passed through PAM components during authentication.

T1556.004.description: Patch network device OS image to include hardcoded backdoor password that grants authentication bypass while still permitting normal credential validation.

T1556.005.description: Enable AD AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption property so passwords are stored recoverably; decrypt using userParameters values, LSA secret, and RASSFM.DLL static key.

T1556.006.description: Disable or modify MFA mechanisms by excluding users from policies, registering attacker MFA methods, or redirecting MFA server traffic to trigger fail-open behavior.

T1556.007.description: Backdoor hybrid identity sync components (PTA agent DLL injection, AD FS Microsoft.IdentityServer DLL, rogue PTA registration) to forge tokens and harvest credentials.

T1556.008.description: Register malicious network provider DLL as credential manager so mpnotify.exe delivers cleartext logon credentials via NPLogonNotify during Windows authentication.

T1556.009.description: Modify conditional access or IAM policies (trusted IPs, MFA requirements, region restrictions) to weaken access controls and maintain persistent account access.

T1557.description: Position between networked devices by abusing ARP/DNS/LLMNR or protocol downgrades to intercept traffic, capture credentials, tokens, cookies, or manipulate data.

T1557.001.description: Respond to LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS broadcasts to spoof name resolution, capture NTLMv1/v2 hashes for cracking, or relay them via SMB/LDAP/HTTP to authenticate.

T1557.002.description: Send forged ARP replies or gratuitous ARP announcements to associate attacker MAC with target IP, redirecting LAN traffic for sniffing or manipulation.

T1557.003.description: Spoof rogue DHCP server responding to client DISCOVER/INFORMATION-REQUEST messages with malicious network configs (DNS, gateway) to redirect traffic through adversary-controlled systems for AiTM.

T1557.004.description: Host fraudulent Wi-Fi access point mimicking legitimate SSID or responding to PNL probe requests, luring devices to connect for traffic interception and credential capture via fake portals.

T1558.description: Steal or forge Kerberos tickets to subvert authentication and enable Pass the Ticket access in Windows domain environments.

T1558.001.description: Forge Kerberos TGTs using stolen KRBTGT account hash, enabling authentication as any AD account and requesting arbitrary TGS tickets from KDC.

T1558.002.description: Forge Kerberos TGS service tickets using a target service account's password hash, granting access to specific services without KDC interaction, evading detection.

T1558.003.description: Request TGS tickets for service SPNs from DC using valid TGT; RC4-encrypted ticket portions contain service account hashes vulnerable to offline brute-force cracking.

T1558.004.description: Identify accounts with Kerberos preauthentication disabled via LDAP, send AS-REQ without timestamp, receive AS-REP containing encrypted material vulnerable to offline password cracking.

T1558.005.description: Steal Kerberos credential cache files from Linux /tmp (krb5cc_UID) or macOS memory (API:{uuid}) to extract TGTs for Pass the Ticket without password.

T1559.description: Abuse OS inter-process communication mechanisms (pipes, sockets, COM, DDE) to execute arbitrary code or commands locally between processes.

T1559.001.description: Invoke Windows COM interfaces to execute code via DLL/EXE server objects, enabling fileless execution, scheduled task creation, and privilege escalation through exposed COM objects.

T1559.002.description: Abuse Windows DDE protocol to execute commands via poisoned Office documents or CSV files, bypassing VBA macros; can be invoked remotely via DCOM.

T1559.003.description: Send malicious content to macOS XPC service daemons running as root via XPC C API or NSXPCConnection, exploiting weak client validation for code execution.

T1560.description: Compress and/or encrypt collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate content and reduce transfer size using utilities, libraries, or custom methods.

T1560.001.description: Use built-in or third-party utilities like tar, zip, 7-Zip, WinRAR, diantz, makecab, or certutil to compress/encrypt data before exfiltration.

T1560.002.description: Use programming libraries such as rarfile, libzip, zlib, or bzip2 linked into code to compress/encrypt collected data without spawning external utility processes.

T1560.003.description: Implement custom encryption (XOR, stream ciphers) or compression algorithms inline without external library references to archive data prior to exfiltration.

T1561.description: Overwrite raw disk sectors or structures like MBR to render systems unbootable; wiper malware may propagate worm-like across networks for mass impact.

T1561.001.description: Overwrite arbitrary portions of disk storage with random data via direct disk access or drivers like RawDisk, rendering content irrecoverable through storage interface.

T1561.002.description: Corrupt boot-critical disk structures like MBR or partition table to prevent OS loading; on network devices, reformat filesystem via `format` command.

T1563.description: Commandeer existing authenticated remote sessions (RDP, SSH, telnet) to laterally move without creating new sessions or supplying credentials.

T1563.001.description: Hijack existing SSH session via compromised ssh-agent or its socket to move laterally using established trust relationships without new authentication.

T1563.002.description: Use tscon.exe with SYSTEM privileges to steal another user's active or disconnected RDP session without credentials or prompts.

T1564.description: Abuse OS features designed to hide files, accounts, or activity from users, including isolated virtualized regions, to evade detection.

T1564.001.description: Mark files/directories hidden via leading dot (Linux/macOS), UF_HIDDEN flag, or attrib.exe +h on Windows to avoid display in default file browsers.

T1564.002.description: Hide accounts from login screens via plist Hide500Users, Windows SpecialAccounts\\UserList=0, dscl IsHidden=1, or GDM disable-user-list.

T1564.003.description: Conceal application windows via powershell -WindowStyle Hidden, plist UIElement, CreateDesktop() API for hVNC, or LOLBins like DeviceCredentialDeployment.exe.

T1564.004.description: Store payloads in NTFS Alternate Data Streams or Extended Attributes within MFT entries to hide binaries from file-scanning AV tools.

T1564.005.description: Implement custom file system in unused disk sectors, dropped partition images, or fragmented across existing FS to hide files from security tools.

T1564.006.description: Execute payloads inside VMs (QEMU, VirtualBox, Hyper-V, Windows Sandbox .wsb, ESXi /bin/vmx) to hide activity from host-based security tools.

T1564.007.description: Overwrite VBA source code in Office module streams with benign data while retaining malicious compiled p-code in PerformanceCache to bypass source scanners.

T1564.008.description: Create email client rules to auto-delete/move inbound messages containing keywords like malware/phish/suspicious to hide alerts, C2 replies, or spearphishing responses.

T1564.009.description: Hide malicious code/data within macOS resource forks accessible via extended attributes; payload extracted at offset, moved to executable location, and invoked.

T1564.010.description: Overwrite Process Environment Block command-line arguments after process creation to hide malicious args from monitoring tools; spawn suspended with benign args then patch.

T1564.011.description: Invoke processes with hangup-immune flags like nohup or PowerShell -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue to survive logoff, errors, or termination signals from defenders.

T1564.012.description: Drop payloads into folders/filenames known to be excluded from antivirus scanning, leveraging hardcoded trusted paths rather than modifying AV settings.

T1564.013.description: Bind-mount a benign /proc/PID directory over a malicious process's /proc entry so ps/top display benign metadata, hiding the malicious process from utilities.

T1564.014.description: Embed second-stage payloads inside file extended attributes (xattrs); loader retrieves with xattr -p or getfattr, decodes, and executes while file hash remains unchanged.

T1565.description: Insert, delete, or modify data to influence outcomes or hide activity, compromising integrity of business processes and decision-making.

T1565.001.description: Modify data at rest in databases, files, or stored emails to influence business processes or conceal activity, requiring knowledge of target data formats.

T1565.002.description: Intercept and alter data in transit between systems/processes to manipulate outcomes or hide activity, requiring deployed interception tooling on network or IPC.

T1565.003.description: Modify application binaries or file associations to alter data as accessed/displayed to users, undermining integrity and influencing decisions without changing stored data.

T1566.description: Send electronic social-engineering messages via email, social media, or callback lures to deliver malicious links/attachments or trick users into executing payloads.

T1566.001.description: Send targeted emails with malicious attachments (Office docs, PDFs, executables, password-protected archives) relying on user execution to trigger exploits or payloads.

T1566.002.description: Send targeted emails containing URLs leading to malware downloads, browser exploits, or OAuth/device-code consent pages to steal tokens.

T1566.003.description: Deliver targeted lures through third-party services (social media, personal webmail) to bypass enterprise email controls and build rapport before sending payloads.

T1566.004.description: Use phone calls/voice communications to socially engineer victims into visiting URLs, installing RMM tools, or approving MFA prompts.

T1567.description: Exfiltrate data via legitimate external web services instead of C2 channel, blending with existing allowed encrypted traffic.

T1567.001.description: Push stolen data to code repository APIs over HTTPS, leveraging trusted developer services for covert exfiltration.

T1567.002.description: Upload stolen data to cloud storage services like Dropbox or Google Drive that blend with normal user traffic.

T1567.003.description: Exfiltrate collected data to text/paste sites like pastebin.com, optionally using paid encryption features for concealment.

T1567.004.description: Exfiltrate data by posting to webhook endpoints on services like Discord, Slack, or webhook.site, blending with normal HTTPS traffic to legitimate SaaS platforms.

T1568.description: Dynamically compute C2 parameters (domain, IP, port) via shared algorithms between malware and infrastructure to evade static detections and reestablish lost channels.

T1568.001.description: Rapidly rotate IP addresses bound to a single FQDN via short TTLs and frequent A/NS record changes to hide C2 infrastructure behind shifting resolutions.

T1568.002.description: Generate large numbers of candidate domains algorithmically (random strings or concatenated words, often time-seeded) for C2 rendezvous, defeating static domain blocking.

T1568.003.description: Compute C2 port/IP from octets of DNS response addresses rather than using the returned values directly, bypassing egress filtering on predetermined ports.

T1569.description: Execute commands or payloads by interacting with or creating local/remote system services or daemons for one-time or persistent execution.

T1569.001.description: Use macOS launchctl to interact with launchd and execute Launch Agents/Daemons via subcommands like load, unload, and start.

T1569.002.description: Abuse Windows Service Control Manager via sc.exe, PsExec, or Net to create/modify/start services for local or remote command execution.

T1569.003.description: Use systemctl to control systemd units, starting, enabling, or invoking Systemd Services to execute commands or payloads on Linux.

T1570.description: Copy tools and files between internal systems using SMB shares, RDP, scp, rsync, sftp, curl, ftp, or synced cloud folders to stage payloads during lateral movement.

T1571.description: Communicate over uncommon protocol/port pairings (e.g., HTTPS on 8088/587) to bypass filtering and evade traffic analysis.

T1572.description: Encapsulate C2 traffic within another protocol (SSH, DoH, HTTPS) to evade filtering, blend with legitimate traffic, and route otherwise blocked protocols.

T1573.description: Apply custom encryption algorithms to C2 traffic beyond protocol-provided protections; keys often embedded in malware enabling reverse engineering.

T1573.001.description: Encrypt C2 traffic using symmetric ciphers (AES/DES/RC4) with shared keys for plaintext encryption and ciphertext decryption.

T1573.002.description: Encrypt C2 traffic using public/private keypair algorithms (RSA, ElGamal); often used in SSL/TLS to exchange symmetric session keys.

T1574.description: Hijack OS mechanisms for locating and loading programs/libraries to execute payloads for persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion.

T1574.001.description: Abuse Windows DLL loading via sideloading, search order hijacking, phantom/missing DLLs, redirection manifests, or substitution to execute payloads under trusted processes.

T1574.004.description: Plant malicious dylib with expected name in macOS application's @rpath search path; weak linking allows missing dylibs to be supplied by attacker.

T1574.005.description: Overwrite binaries unpacked by installers into %TEMP% subdirectories with weak permissions; replaced binary executes at installer's elevated privilege.

T1574.006.description: Set linker environment variables (LD_PRELOAD/DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES) to preload malicious shared libraries, hooking libc functions to hide artifacts and inherit process privileges.

T1574.007.description: Place malicious binary in directory listed earlier in PATH than legitimate executable, or modify PATH/HOME variables to point to attacker-writable directory, causing OS to execute malicious file when unqualified name is called.

T1574.008.description: Abuse Windows search order for programs called without full path by placing malicious executable (e.g., net.com before net.exe via PATHEXT) in the initiating program's directory to be loaded preferentially.

T1574.009.description: Exploit service or shortcut paths containing spaces without surrounding quotes by placing executable at higher directory level (e.g., C:\program.exe intercepts C:\program files\myapp.exe).

T1574.010.description: Exploit weak file/directory permissions on Windows service binaries to overwrite the executable with a malicious one, which runs under the service's elevated context (often SYSTEM) at startup.

T1574.011.description: Modify weakly-permissioned service Registry keys (ImagePath, FailureCommand, Performance, Parameters) to redirect execution to attacker-controlled binary or DLL loaded when service starts or fails.

T1574.012.description: Set COR_PROFILER environment variable or Registry COM entry to load a malicious unmanaged DLL into any .NET process loading the CLR, enabling persistence, privilege escalation, and defense impairment.

T1574.013.description: Hijack process execution by locating KernelCallbackTable via PEB, duplicating it with a callback (e.g., fnCOPYDATA) pointing to malicious payload, and updating PEB pointer; payload triggers on Windows message dispatch.

T1574.014.description: Hijack .NET assembly loading by abusing AppDomainManager class via tampered .config files or environment variables, instructing benign .NET apps to load malicious assembly into target process.

T1578.description: Create, delete, or modify cloud compute components (VMs, snapshots, volumes) to bypass access restrictions, evade detection, and remove evidence within victim cloud accounts.

T1578.001.description: Create a snapshot of an existing cloud VM, disk, or volume to bypass restrictions on the original resource, often mounting the snapshot to an attacker-controlled instance for data access.

T1578.002.description: Create new cloud VM to bypass existing instance security controls; mount snapshots of victim volumes under less restrictive policies to access data without affecting running instances.

T1578.003.description: Delete cloud VM/instance after operations to remove forensic artifacts and evidence of activity, especially instances created for malicious purposes.

T1578.004.description: Restore VM/data from snapshots or use ephemeral storage that resets on stop/restart to erase evidence of post-compromise activity in cloud environments.

T1578.005.description: Alter cloud compute settings—service quotas, tenant policies, subscription associations—to expand available resources for hijacking without exhausting victim quotas or alerting them.

T1580.description: Enumerate IaaS resources (instances, snapshots, buckets, databases) via cloud APIs/CLI like AWS DescribeInstances, ListBuckets, gcloud compute instances list, az vm list.

T1583.description: Buy, lease, or rent infrastructure (servers, domains, botnets, web services) including free trials to stage and launch operations while obscuring attribution.

T1583.001.description: Register domains for phishing, drive-by, or C2 use, including lookalike/homoglyph/IDN domains, expired allowlisted domains, or domains registered in compromised cloud accounts.

T1583.002.description: Provision own DNS servers to control server-side DNS C2 traffic, enabling conditional malware responses and flexible DNS-based command channel structures.

T1583.003.description: Rent VPS from cloud providers (often with minimal registration) to host operations, leveraging provider reputation and rapid provisioning while hindering attribution.

T1583.004.description: Buy or lease physical servers to host watering holes, phishing, or C2 infrastructure rather than compromising third-party servers or using VPS providers.

T1583.005.description: Purchase/lease network of compromised systems via booter/stresser services or operational relay box (ORB) networks of VPS/SOHO/IoT devices for phishing, DDoS, or C2 proxying.

T1583.006.description: Register accounts on legitimate web services (GitHub, Google, Twitter) to blend C2, exfiltration, or phishing traffic with expected noise and obscure attribution.

T1583.007.description: Acquire serverless cloud functions (Lambda, Workers, Apps Script) to proxy or respond to victim traffic, appearing as legitimate cloud provider subdomains.

T1583.008.description: Purchase online ads to position trojanized software clones in search results, impersonate brands, and use cloaking to route crawlers to benign pages while victims hit malicious sites.

T1584.description: Compromise third-party servers, domains, DNS, or network devices to stage operations, blend with trusted traffic, build botnets, or enable Wi-Fi proximity access.

T1584.001.description: Hijack domains via registrar account compromise, social engineering, or DNS provider takeover; exploit dangling DNS records for subdomain takeover or create shadow subdomains.

T1584.002.description: Compromise third-party DNS servers to alter records, redirect victim traffic, pair with rogue certificates, prove domain ownership to SaaS, or create stealthy malicious subdomains.

T1584.003.description: Compromise VPSs owned by third parties to host staging or C2, leveraging trust of major cloud providers and obscuring attribution through victim ownership.

T1584.004.description: Compromise third-party physical/web/email servers to stage payloads, host watering hole content, relay phishing, or operate C2 infrastructure.

T1584.005.description: Build a botnet by compromising numerous third-party hosts, or hijack an existing botnet by redirecting bots to attacker-controlled C2 for DDoS or mass phishing.

T1584.006.description: Compromise legitimate users' third-party web service accounts (GitHub, Google, Twitter, Dropbox) to blend with expected traffic for later C2, exfiltration, or phishing operations.

T1584.007.description: Compromise serverless cloud functions (AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, Google Apps Script) to proxy C2 traffic via trusted cloud provider subdomains, obscuring attribution.

T1584.008.description: Compromise third-party network devices like SOHO routers and edge appliances lacking host defenses to host payloads, proxy C2, harvest credentials, or enable content injection.

T1585.description: Create and cultivate accounts on social media, email, or cloud services to build personas supporting social engineering, phishing, or free-tier infrastructure abuse.

T1585.002.description: Register email accounts (including disposable services) to send phishing, support persona credibility, and register for domain/cloud infrastructure trial services.

T1585.003.description: Register cloud provider accounts to host C2, exfiltrate data to cloud storage, upload tools, or acquire VPS/serverless infrastructure without managing own servers.

T1586.002.description: Take over existing email accounts via phishing, breach dumps, or insider access to hijack reply threads, send phishing from trusted senders, and bypass reputation filtering.

T1586.003.description: Compromise cloud accounts via phishing, password spraying, or token theft to leverage cloud storage, messaging, and compute for staging, exfiltration, and C2.

T1587.description: Build custom capabilities including malware, exploits, and certificates in-house rather than purchasing or downloading, tailored to operational requirements.

T1587.002.description: Generate self-signed code signing certificates to sign executables/scripts, lending perceived authenticity prior to deploying signed payloads.

T1587.004.description: Develop custom exploits targeting known or discovered vulnerabilities via fuzzing and patch analysis for use across multiple lifecycle phases.

T1588.description: Acquire capabilities (malware, tools, exploits, certificates, vuln info) through purchase, free download, or theft from third parties or other actors.

T1588.002.description: Acquire legitimate or commercial software tools (PsExec, Cobalt Strike) via download, purchase, theft, or cracking for post-compromise operations.

T1588.005.description: Acquire exploits via purchase from vendors/marketplaces, download from public sources, or theft from researchers and other actors for use across multiple lifecycle phases.

T1588.006.description: Obtain vulnerability information from public databases (NVD), closed sources, or targeting researchers to identify weaknesses for exploit development or acquisition.

T1588.007.description: Leverage generative AI/LLMs to draft phishing content, generate scripts/payloads, automate recon, obfuscate code, and create deepfake media for impersonation.

T1589.description: Collect victim identity data including personal details, credentials, and MFA configurations via phishing, authentication probing, or open data sets.

T1589.001.description: Harvest victim credentials via phishing, breach dumps, dark web markets, infostealer Telegram channels, MFA/OTP provider compromise, or code repository leaks.
